title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E510 asks how tall a column can be before it buckles under its own weight. In §13 Euler treated a crude model that can bend only at its mid-point (hinge stiffness Ee) and got a critical height b = √(8Ee/dd). From §14 he takes up the continuous elastic column. He applies a small fictitious horizontal load C, spread uniformly as C dx/b per element, to make the column bow into a continuous curve.

This page completes the inventory of forces (free-body set-up for the pinned–pinned, self-weighted column):
(i) Each element carries its weight M dx/b vertically downward, where M is the total weight.
(ii) The bending stiffness is written Ekk, so the bending moment equals Ekk/r.
(iii) The top end A is kept on the vertical line by a horizontal reaction A, and the bottom end B by a horizontal reaction B.
(iv) The bottom end also carries an upward vertical reaction M.
(v) For global equilibrium the distributed weight is replaced by its resultant M acting at the centre of gravity G of the bent column. With AX = x and XY = y, small deflection lets the arc element Yy be taken equal to dx. Each element then has moment (M dx/b)·y about the axis AB. Hence M·GO = (M/b)∫y dx, i.e. GO = (1/b)∫₀ᵇ y dx: the mean deflection, equal to the area under the curve AYB divided by b.

On the next page these give:
- Horizontal equilibrium: A + B = C.
- Moments about A: B·b + M·g = ½Cb, with g = GO.
- Hence B = ½C − Mg/b and A = ½C + Mg/b.

The local moment balance at a section Y (§17) then leads to the differential equation for the elastica. The standard modern problem is EI y'' + q x y' + … = 0, which reduces to Bessel/Airy-type functions (Greenhill 1881).
errors: The weight resultant at G is called 'vis ... horizontalis Gg = M'. Weight is vertical, and on the next page Euler himself treats Gg = M as balancing the vertical reaction BO = M. So 'horizontalis' is a slip for 'verticalis'.
No error in the mean-deflection formula GO = (1/b)∫y dx. Under the small-deflection linearization (arc length ≈ dx) it is correct.

Using the resultant at G is valid for global moment equilibrium. For the local moment at Y, however, the weight of the part AY above the section must be used, with its own centroid; this is handled on later pages. Euler's final results in this 1778 paper on self-weight buckling are generally regarded as defective (Truesdell's assessment). The correct critical heights came with Greenhill (1881).

ideas.what: Free-body equilibrium of a self-weighted pinned–pinned column, with horizontal end reactions and an upward base reaction
ideas.modern_name: statics of a beam-column under distributed axial load
ideas.where_published: E510 and companion 1778 column papers (E508, E509)

ideas.what: Horizontal offset of the centre of gravity of the bent column equals the mean deflection (1/b)∫y dx
ideas.modern_name: centroid of a slightly deflected rod; small-deflection linearization

ideas.what: Using a small fictitious distributed lateral load C to excite a continuous buckling mode
ideas.usually_credited_to: various; Euler used lateral-load devices in column theory

deep.surprise_reason: This page is a routine statics set-up: force inventory and centroid of the deflected column. The self-weight buckling problem and Euler's flawed treatment of it are well documented (Truesdell, Greenhill). Nothing here is new.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image well; the 'horizontalis' in the last line is in the original print (an Euler/printer slip), not a transcription error.
